slides.title: Predicates and quantifiers
slides.sub: Chapter 6 · Speaking about all cases at once
slides.main: "The code works for all inputs" — that is exactly what you prove with each of your tests.

captions: Predicates and quantifiers
Every day you write conditions: the user is an admin, the array is not empty, the response arrived in time
Behind them stands a strict language that lets you talk about all the cases at once, not one by one
Two main tools: predicates — statements with a variable — and the quantifiers "for every" and "there exists"
Without them you cannot explain what "the code works for all inputs" means — you prove that with every test

body.text: If the user is an admin, if the array is not empty, if the response arrived in time — behind these lines stands the strict language of quantifiers.

slides.title: What a predicate is
slides.sub: The phrase "x is greater than five" is neither true nor false
slides.main: A predicate is a function that takes a value and returns a boolean.

captions: "x is greater than five" is neither true nor false: it hangs in the air until x is known
Such a template with a variable is a predicate: substitute a value and you get an ordinary statement
"Age is greater than 18": for 20 — true, for 15 — false
Nothing mystical: a function that takes a value and returns a bool

body.text: "Age is greater than eighteen" gives true for twenty and false for fifteen. Nothing mystical: a template with a variable.

slides.title: Predicates in your code
slides.sub: You use them constantly, you just rarely say the word
slides.main: As soon as you see statements with a variable in them, you have a language for strict reasoning.

captions: You use predicates constantly, you just rarely say the word
filter takes a predicate and keeps only the elements on which it is true
find looks for the first element on which the predicate becomes true
The condition inside an if is the same predicate over the variables of the program's state
Seeing statements with a variable in such functions gives you a language in which they can be reasoned about strictly

frames.text: first match: 12 — we don't look further
P(x): a statement with a variable

body.text: Three different methods — one and the same device: a function-statement with a variable that decides the fate of each element or branch.

slides.title: The universal quantifier: for every
slides.sub: The first way to turn a predicate into a statement
slides.main: A statement about everyone cannot be proved with a couple of cases — you need an argument that works for any value.

captions: How to turn predicates into complete statements
The first way is the universal quantifier: "for every", "for all"
For every x it is true that x + 0 = x — we get a statement that is true or false
"All passengers are buckled up" is about each one without exception; one unbuckled is enough to refute it
A statement about everyone cannot be proved by a couple of cases — a general argument for any value is needed

body.text: "All passengers are buckled up" is about each one without exception. For every x: x plus zero equals x — true about all values at once.

slides.title: The existential quantifier: there exists
slides.sub: The second way to turn a predicate into a statement
slides.main: Proving existence is easy — one example is enough; refuting it is harder.

captions: The second way is the existential quantifier: "there exists", "there is"
"Among the guests there is a vegetarian" is true if at least one fits
Proving it is easy — one example is enough, that is its charm
Refuting it is harder: you have to explain why nobody fits
Proving that a bug exists is one reproduction; that there are no bugs is a different conversation

frames.text: one fitting guest — and the statement is proved
you must check everyone: nobody fits
proving "no bugs" means examining all the cases

slides.title: Quantifiers in tests
slides.sub: A unit test is existence, property-based is universality
slides.main: One counterexample is stronger: no matter how many green runs cover for it.

captions: It is time to see quantifiers in your own tests
A unit test is an existence statement: on these three inputs the function answers correctly
Property-based is the quantifier "for all": on all the generated inputs the property must hold
A "for all" statement is refuted by one counterexample
One failed input is enough — and the property is violated, no matter how many green runs cover for it

frames.text: ∃ three inputs where all is right
a thousand green runs do not prove "for all"

slides.title: Negation rules for quantifiers
slides.main: Negation honestly moves inside, flipping the quantifier to the opposite one.

captions: Quantifiers have negation rules, and they are surprisingly practical
It is not true that "all are buckled up" ⇒ there is an unbuckled one
It is not true that "there is a vegetarian" ⇒ every guest eats meat
De Morgan's mirrors: negation goes inside, flipping the quantifier to the opposite one
No magic — just a careful translation from English into English

frames.text: the quantifier changes, the negation goes inside

body.text: No magic — just a careful translation from English into English.

slides.title: The flip: some and every
slides.main: The formulas tell you how to rewrite the phrase without getting dizzy.

captions: In code the same rule looks like a flip
It is not true that every passed the check — so there is an element that failed: that is some with a negation
"The predicate is not true for all" is harder to read than "there is an element where it is false", though the meaning is one
In review: notice double negations and untangle them with this rule

frames.text: the same thing: a failing one was found

"not for all elements
the predicate is true"

"there is an element
where it is false"

body.text: A useful skill in review is to notice double negations and untangle them with this rule.

slides.title: The order of quantifiers changes the meaning
slides.short: The order of quantifiers changes the meaning
slides.main: A mixed-up order of quantifiers is a classic source of errors in requirements and interfaces.

captions: The order of quantifiers changes the meaning — here logic really bites
"Every person has a mother": for every x there is its own y — trivially true
"There is a person who is the mother of everyone": one y for all — absurd
∀x ∃y: y is chosen for each x; ∃y ∀x: one y for everyone
A mixed-up order is a classic source of errors in requirements and interfaces

frames.text: y is chosen for each x — "its own"
one y is chosen for everyone
mixed up the order — and "everyone waits" for one hero

body.text: In the second case one y is chosen for everyone, in the first each x gets its own. The meaning changes from the order of the symbols alone.

slides.title: Quantifiers in requirements
slides.sub: The order of quantifiers is part of the contract
slides.main: Write the quantifiers out explicitly before arguing at planning — often people argue about different formulas.

captions: Let's carry this over into the language of development
"For every request there is a handler" is normal: each type gets its own handler
"There is a handler for every request" is a universal stub that responds identically to everything
Requirements almost always contain hidden quantifiers, and their order is part of the contract
Before arguing at planning, write the quantifiers out explicitly — often people argue about different formulas

frames.text: "there is a server for all clients"

body.text: Requirements for a system almost always contain hidden quantifiers, and sound similar but mean different things.

slides.title: Restricting the domain of a quantifier
slides.sub: Not "for all in general", but "for all from…"
slides.short: Restricting the domain of a quantifier
slides.main: The test checks the quantifier not over the whole world but over the domain of the generator.

captions: In practice quantifiers are almost always restricted to a domain: not "for all x in general"
The restriction is the familiar filter before the check: we take not the whole world but the set we need
In property-based tests generators play the restriction: numbers 0…100, non-empty strings, valid JSON
The subtlety: the test checks the quantifier not over the whole world but over the domain of the generator
If the generator does not produce negative numbers, "for all numbers" has been checked only for the positive ones

frames.text: generators set the domain of the quantifier

slides.title: A pocket debugging reference
slides.sub: From which side it is cheaper to attack a statement
slides.main: Logic tells you which refutation costs one run and which costs a general argument.

captions: Let's put together a pocket reference
"For all" is proved by a general argument and destroyed by one counterexample
"There exists" is proved by one example and destroyed by a general argument
Debugging: to refute "the function is correct" — look for a minimal counterexample; "always crashes" — one successful run is enough
Logic tells you from which side it is cheaper to attack a statement

frames.text:
"correct" → look for a counterexample
"always crashes" → one successful run
green is cheap, red is expensive

body.text: The strategy: to refute "the function is correct", look for a minimal counterexample; to refute "the function always crashes", one successful run is enough.

slides.title: Summary: quantifiers in practice
slides.main: One counterexample is stronger than a thousand green runs.

captions: Summing up the chapter
A predicate is a statement with a variable: a template that becomes true or false on substitution
The quantifiers "for every" and "there exists" turn templates into statements; negation flips the quantifier
The order of quantifiers is part of the meaning: a mixed-up order changes the contract
Tests are quantifiers in practice: unit — "there exists", property-based — "for all"; one counterexample is stronger than a thousand green runs
